itens.resumo: Eleventh-century cardinal-bishop whose gesture in Constantinople in 1054 is traditionally pointed to as the landmark of the Schism between Rome and the Christian East.
itens.corpo:
Born around the year 1000, according to some sources closer to 1015, in the region of Lorraine (some say he was a native of Burgundy), then part of the Holy Roman Empire, Humbert entered at the age of fifteen as an oblate at the Benedictine monastery of Moyenmoutier, in the Vosges, where he professed monastic vows according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and came to be elected abbot. There he trained in Greek and Latin — a rare skill among Latin clerics of the eleventh century, and one that would prove decisive in the disputes with Constantinople — and directed his theological studies above all to the question of the relations between ecclesiastical power and secular power, a theme that would mark all of his later activity.

His friendship with Bruno of Toul, a bishop who would become pope under the name Leo IX in 1049, changed the course of his life: Bruno took him to Rome as a direct collaborator. In 1050 Leo IX even appointed him Archbishop of Sicily, a post that the Norman rulers of the island prevented him from taking up; in its place, Humbert was created cardinal-bishop of the suburbicarian see of Silva Candida (Santa Rufina) in 1051 — becoming, according to some historians, the first Frenchman to receive the cardinal's biretta — and began to serve as chief papal secretary, becoming the most influential executor of the policy of ecclesiastical reform of Leo IX and, after him, of Victor II, Stephen IX and Nicholas II. He stood at Leo IX's side even in defeat: he was taken prisoner with the pope by the Normans at the Battle of Civitate (1053) and spent about nine months detained with him in Benevento.

As a theologian of the reform, Humbert turned with particular vehemence against two evils that he saw eating away at the Church of his time: simony, that is, the buying and selling of ecclesiastical offices, and Nicolaitism, the concubinage of the clergy. These concerns would come to maturity in his most influential work, the treatise «Libri tres adversus Simoniacos» («Three Books Against the Simoniacs»), written around 1057, one of the programmatic texts of the Gregorian reform that would be consolidated under Pope Gregory VII, decades later. His radical position — that ordinations and sacraments conferred by simoniacal clerics would be invalid — met with opposition within the reform movement itself, and was refuted by Peter Damian; the two are, however, frequently cited side by side as the principal reformers of the eleventh century.

In 1053, while traveling through Apulia, Humbert received a letter from Archbishop Leo of Ohrid harshly criticizing liturgical and disciplinary practices of the West, among them the use of unleavened bread (azymes) in the Eucharist and fasting on Saturdays — differences which, added to old disputes over Roman primacy and over the «Filioque» clause in the Creed, had for centuries been feeding the estrangement between Rome and Constantinople. He translated the letter into Latin, delivered it to the pope, and himself drafted a reply, the treatise «Adversus Graecorum calumnias» («Against the Calumnies of the Greeks»). The exchange of accusations led Leo IX to send, in 1054, a legation to Constantinople to negotiate with Patriarch Michael Cerularius, who had also closed the Latin-rite churches in the city. Humbert led this mission, accompanied by Frederick of Lorraine — the future Pope Stephen IX — and by Peter, Archbishop of Amalfi.

Pope Leo IX died on April 19, 1054, before the mission was concluded, which technically terminated the legates' mandate; even so, Humbert and his companions remained in Constantinople and continued the theological discussions, now with no authority other than their own. Frustrated by the impasse and by the Greek refusal to accept his demands for submission to the Latin Church, Humbert drew up a bull (charta excommunicationis) against Patriarch Michael Cerularius, accusing him of heresy, and on July 16, 1054, during the celebration of the divine liturgy, he laid it upon the high altar of the Basilica of Hagia Sophia — a gesture accompanied by a condemnation of a general tone that extended to the whole Greek Church. It is said that, on leaving the church, he shook the dust from his feet, saying: «May God see and judge».

Four days later, on July 20, 1054, a synod convened by Michael Cerularius, with about twenty-one metropolitans and bishops, responded by excommunicating not all of Western Christendom, but specifically the three Roman legates — a distinction that later memory would tend to erase, simplifying the episode as a mutual excommunication between the two entire Churches. Two days afterward, the papal delegation left Constantinople for Rome. The act, of questionable juridical validity — given that the pope who had authorized the mission had already died — became, over time, the symbolic landmark of the Great Schism of the East, although the estrangement between the two Churches was, in reality, a gradual process, woven over centuries by liturgical, disciplinary, linguistic and political differences, and only formally overcome in part when Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I mutually lifted the excommunications of 1054, on December 7, 1965.

Back in Rome, Humbert continued to serve the Curia: Pope Stephen IX, his former companion on the legation, appointed him librarian and chancellor. He is credited with a decisive role in the formulation of the electoral decree of 1059 («In Nomine Domini»), by which papal election came to be reserved to the cardinals, with a preponderant role for the cardinal-bishops — although historians debate the real extent of his hand in the text, which was also the work of other collaborators of Nicholas II. Humbert died in Rome on May 5, 1061, and was buried in the Lateran Basilica.

itens.resumo: German cardinal of the fifteenth century, philosopher and theologian of "learned ignorance," a central figure of Christian humanism in the transition between the Middle Ages and the Renaissance.
itens.corpo:
Nicholas Krebs was born in 1401 in Kues, on the banks of the Moselle, the son of a prosperous boatman and raftsman who was able to pay for an education unusual for the time. He studied at the preparatory school of the Brothers of the Common Life in Deventer, entered the Faculty of Arts of the University of Heidelberg in 1416, and earned a doctorate in canon law in Padua in 1423, where he formed friendships with two future cardinals, Giuliano Cesarini and Domenico Capranica, and with the mathematician Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli — a companionship that would mark his lasting interest in mathematics and astronomy. He completed his formation at the University of Cologne from 1425 and, back in his native region, served as secretary to the Archbishop-Elector Otto von Ziegenhain, becoming a canon and dean of the chapter of Koblenz.

Already in this period he revealed the philological rigor that would mark his whole work: in 1433, through textual criticism, he demonstrated that the "Donation of Constantine" — a document that served as the legal basis for the temporal claims of the papacy — was a medieval forgery, a conclusion that the humanist Lorenzo Valla would confirm independently shortly afterward. He took part in the Council of Basel (1432-1438) representing rival claimants to the archiepiscopal see of Trier, and there he wrote his first major work, "De Concordantia Catholica," in which he sought to balance hierarchical authority and conciliar consensus in the governance of the Church and the Empire. Initially a conciliarist, he gradually moved away from that position, maintaining that the assembly of Basel did not have universal ecclesial consensus to place itself above the pope; between 1437 and 1438 he was part of the delegation sent to Constantinople to bring the Byzantine emperor to the Council of Ferrara-Florence, a journey during which he claimed to have experienced, aboard the ship on the return voyage, an experience of spiritual illumination that would directly inspire his most famous philosophical work.

Created cardinal by Nicholas V in 1448 or 1449, he was appointed Prince-Bishop of Bressanone (Brixen), in Tyrol, in 1450, and in the same year received a commission as papal legate for the German lands, at the head of the so-called "Great Legation" (1450-1452): nearly five thousand kilometers traveled in preaching, teaching, and ecclesiastical reform, which earned him from his contemporaries the epithet "Hercules of the Eugenian cause" (loyal to the pope of Rome, Eugene IV, against conciliarism). As Bishop of Brixen, between 1452 and 1458, he imposed disciplinary reforms and tried to recover alienated diocesan revenues, which put him on a collision course with Duke Sigismund of Tyrol, who was also displeased with Nicholas's ecclesiastical appointments. The conflict worsened until the cardinal's imprisonment in 1460; in retaliation, Pope Pius II excommunicated the duke and placed an interdict on his lands. Nicholas would never in fact regain effective government of the diocese, withdrawing to Rome, although Sigismund capitulated shortly after the cardinal's death.

As a thinker, he is known above all for his doctrine of "learned ignorance" ("De Docta Ignorantia," 1440): the certainty that the finite human intellect never fully attains the essence of the infinite God — the "Maximum" — and that to recognize lucidly the limits of one's own knowledge is already, paradoxically, a higher form of wisdom, grounded both in Neoplatonism and in apophatic theology. After the fall of Constantinople in 1453, he wrote "De Pace Fidei," a visionary dialogue in which representatives of different peoples and religions debate, in an imagined heavenly council, the foundations of a "single religion in a variety of rites" — a work that respected non-Christian traditions without giving up the centrality of Christ. In the same year he composed "De Visione Dei," a meditation on the mystical vision of God written at the request of Benedictine monks.

His speculation also touched on science: he maintained, decades before Copernicus, that the Earth is not the immobile center of the universe, but a body in motion like the others; he also proposed a method of counting the pulse by means of water clocks, a precursor of timed clinical observation, and formulated, as early as 1433, a points-based voting system similar to the one that the mathematician Jean-Charles de Borda would develop independently three centuries later — a proposal that the Church of his time did not adopt. Politically, he held that all legitimate authority arises from the consent of the governed, an idea that would echo far beyond his century.

Nicholas died on August 11, 1464, in Todi, in Umbria, on his way to a papal mission. He was buried in San Pietro in Vincoli in Rome — a tomb now lost, although the relief sculpted by Andrea Bregno in his memory remains there — but, by his own wish, his heart was taken to Kues, to the chapel of the hospice he had founded for the poor elderly of the region, the Cusanusstift, a charitable institution that survives to this day and that preserves, together with the legacy of his personal library, one of the most important collections of medieval manuscripts in Germany. A lunar crater was given his name in recognition of the breadth of his intellectual contribution.

itens.resumo: Spanish cardinal, Archbishop of Toledo, reformer of the clergy, founder of the University of Alcalá, Grand Inquisitor, and twice regent of Castile.
itens.corpo:
Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros was born in 1436 in Torrelaguna, in Castile, the son of the hidalgos Alfonso Jiménez de Cisneros and María de la Torre; he received the name Gonzalo at baptism. He studied at the Studium generale of Alcalá de Henares and at the University of Salamanca, where he obtained a bachelor's degree in law in 1456. In 1459 he went to Rome to practice as a consistorial advocate, where he attracted the attention of Pope Pius II, and he returned to Spain in 1465 with a papal letter guaranteeing him the first vacant benefice; this turned out to be that of Uceda, but the Archbishop of Toledo, Alfonso Carrillo de Acuña, refused to recognize him. Back in Spain, he entered the Order of Friars Minor of the Observance, adopting a regime of extreme austerity: strict fasting, the hairshirt, and an initial refusal of any prominent office. It was this reputation for spiritual rigor that drew the attention of the court: he became personal confessor to Queen Isabella the Catholic, a position he held until the sovereign's death in 1504, and through which he came to influence the decisions of the Castilian Crown directly.

On 20 February 1495 he was appointed Archbishop of Toledo, the primatial see of Spain and one of the richest in Christendom. He at first tried to refuse the appointment, and took possession only after his consecration on 11 October 1495 at the hands of Hernando de Talavera. At the head of the archdiocese, he imposed rigorous reforms on both the secular clergy and the religious orders, including the Franciscans themselves: he demanded effective residence of pastors in their parishes, required an end to clerical concubinage (so-called Nicolaitism), and ordered the religious to observe the original rules of their orders without the dispensations accumulated over the centuries. This policy provoked open resistance in some convents, to the point that friars fled to North Africa to escape the imposed discipline. He also edited the first printed editions of the missal (1500) and the breviary (1502) of the Mozarabic rite.

His career also had a darker and more controversial side. Summoned to Granada at the end of 1499 to support the evangelization of the remaining Muslims of the former Nasrid kingdom, Cisneros broke with the gradual and respectful approach followed until then by the first Archbishop of Granada, Hernando de Talavera, who had learned Arabic and relied on patient catechesis, and adopted methods of direct coercion: he had Muslim leaders who resisted conversion imprisoned and mistreated until they yielded. He then ordered the public burning, in the Bib-Rambla square, of Arabic manuscripts confiscated from mosques, schools, libraries, and private homes; the exact date is uncertain, and the sources place it between 1499 and 1500. The chronicler Juan de Vallejo, a friend and direct witness of the episode, records that the Qur'ans and other books collected from the alfaquis «numbered more than four or five thousand volumes», burned in great bonfires, sparing only the medical texts, about forty volumes, which Cisneros had taken to the library of Alcalá de Henares. The indignation of the Muslim population culminated in the Morisco revolt of the Alpujarras (1499-1501), suppressed by imposing on the rebels the choice between baptism or exile, an episode that in practice contradicted the terms of religious tolerance established in the Treaty of Granada of 1491. He was created cardinal on 17 May 1507 by Pope Julius II, in the same year he assumed the office of Inquisitor General of Castile, a position he would hold with the same disciplinary severity as his diocesan government. In 1509 he personally organized and financed a military expedition that conquered the North African city of Oran, an episode that united his ambition for a crusade against Islam with the strategic interests of the Crown.

His most lasting legacy, however, is intellectual: he founded the University of Alcalá de Henares, gathering there the foremost humanists, theologians, and Hebraists of his time, with chairs devoted both to Scotist and nominalist theology and to the Oriental languages. Under his direction and personal financing, this team of scholars produced the «Complutensian Polyglot Bible», completed in 1517 and published around 1520-1522: a critical edition of Scripture that presented the Hebrew, Greek, Aramaic, and Latin texts side by side in parallel columns, one of the great monuments of biblical scholarship of the European Renaissance and a project that anticipated, in several respects, the methods of modern biblical philology.

Cisneros also played a political role of the first magnitude: he governed Castile as regent on two occasions, appointed by Ferdinand the Catholic. The first regency, in 1506-1507, came about because of the incapacity of Queen Joanna the Mad after the death of Philip the Handsome, until Ferdinand's arrival; the second and more decisive took place between 1516 and 1517, after Ferdinand's death, when, already an octogenarian, he organized troops to quell urban revolts and the opposition of dissident nobles, securing the peaceful succession of the young Charles of Habsburg, grandson of Ferdinand and Isabella and future Emperor Charles V, to the throne of Castile. Cisneros was preparing to receive and advise the new king when the latter finally landed in Spain in September 1517, but he died on the way to that meeting, on 8 November 1517, in Roa de Duero, without ever meeting in person the sovereign whose accession he had secured.

itens.resumo: English cardinal (created by Leo X in 1515) and Lord Chancellor of Henry VIII, the most powerful man in England after the king until he fell from favor for failing to obtain the annulment of the royal marriage.
itens.corpo:
Son of Robert Wolsey of Ipswich and Joan Daundy, Thomas Wolsey was born around March 1473. The tradition that presents him as a butcher's son became a weapon in the hands of his enemies when he amassed wealth and power, but modern studies qualify his humble origins: his father had several businesses and his mother was related to the influential Wingfield and Daundy families, and it was with the support of his uncle Edmund Daundy that Wolsey attended the schools of Ipswich and Magdalen College School and then the University of Oxford, where he distinguished himself by his precocity — he took his degree at about the age of fifteen. He was ordained a priest on March 10, 1498, was chaplain to Henry VII in the last years of his reign and, already at the court of the young Henry VIII, became royal almoner in November 1509.

His ecclesiastical rise went hand in hand with politics. He organized the English expedition against France in 1513 and, on the king's own recommendation, Pope Leo X made him Bishop of Lincoln in February 1514 and Archbishop of York in September of the same year — the second see of the kingdom. On September 10, 1515, Leo X created him a cardinal, with the title of Cardinal-Priest of Santa Cecilia, giving him precedence over all the English clergy, including the Archbishop of Canterbury, William Warham, who had consecrated him bishop. In December 1515 he became Lord Chancellor; in 1518 he received the papal legation «a latere», with a practically permanent character and an ecclesiastical jurisdiction overlapping that of all the bishops of the kingdom. The accumulation of ecclesiastical offices — so-called pluralism — was remarkable even by the standards of the time: besides York, he was administrator of Bath and Wells (1518–1523), of Durham (1523–1530) and of Winchester (1529–1530), Bishop of Tournai and Abbot of St Albans. This monopolization of power and revenues, together with his connection to Rome, made him the most envied and hated man in England and fed the anticlerical sentiment that, after his fall, would be one of the fuels of the English Reformation. His contemporaries nicknamed him «the other king», and the Latin phrase «Ego et rex meus» («I and my king») — placing himself before the sovereign — remained a symbol of his arrogance.

As chancellor, Wolsey expanded the jurisdiction of the Court of Star Chamber, used to prosecute perjury, fraud and abuses by local nobles in favor of poorer subjects, and created the Court of Requests for cases of lesser value. He appointed commissions against the illegal enclosure of common lands («enclosures»), which led to proceedings against 264 landowners — a policy abandoned as early as 1523, when he had to concentrate on collecting subsidies for the king's wars against France, taxing nobility and clergy. He conducted English diplomacy in episodes of great theatricality, such as the meeting between Henry VIII and Francis I of France at the Field of the Cloth of Gold (1520). In his personal life he did not observe clerical chastity: he had a son, Thomas Wynter, and a daughter, Dorothy, for whom he sought to secure ecclesiastical careers and advantageous marriages — matters commented on by contemporaries and later turned into an anticlerical argument. He accumulated a fortune comparable to that of the Crown, financed works and foundations and, from 1514, built Hampton Court Palace on the site of an old manor house of the Hospitallers, enlarging it until it surpassed the royal residences in sumptuousness; in 1528 he gave it to the king, trying in vain to regain his favor. In 1528 he founded a grammar school in Ipswich and, in 1525, Cardinal College in Oxford, on the lands of the suppressed Augustinian priory of St. Frideswide — to finance it, he suppressed about 29 monasteries, whose revenues he assigned to the new institution; after his fall the college would be refounded as King Henry VIII's College and, later, would become the present Christ Church.

His ruin began with the king's «Great Matter» («the King's Great Matter»): the annulment of Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon, which had dragged on since 1527 without Pope Clement VII, under pressure from Emperor Charles V, Catherine's nephew, being willing to grant it. On May 31, 1529, the legatine court presided over by Wolsey and the papal legate Lorenzo Campeggio opened at Blackfriars, London, to judge the case; Catherine of Aragon appeared and appealed directly to Rome, and the case was finally revoked to the Holy See, leaving the king without a decision. Wolsey's failure paved the way for the definitive break with Rome and for the Church of England under royal supremacy, consummated by the Act of Supremacy of 1534.

Removed from the chancellorship in October 1529 and indicted for «praemunire» — the charge of having exercised papal authority to the detriment of royal jurisdiction —, Wolsey withdrew first to Esher and then to York, trying to rebuild his ecclesiastical base. Arrested in November 1530 on suspicion of treason, linked to alleged correspondence with the French court, he died on the way to London, at Leicester, on November 29, 1530, before being formally tried, and was buried in the local abbey. His last words, recorded by his biographer and former servant George Cavendish, became famous as the epitaph of his career: «If I had served God as diligently as I have done the king, He would not have given me over in my grey hairs». The phrase, also transmitted by Edward Hall's chronicle, would be reproduced almost literally by Shakespeare in the play «Henry VIII».

itens.resumo: English cardinal of royal blood, exiled for opposing Henry VIII's break with Rome; he returned as papal legate to reconcile the England of Mary I with the Catholic Church, and was the last Catholic Archbishop of Canterbury.
itens.corpo:
Born on March 12, 1500, at Stourton Castle in Staffordshire, Reginald Pole was the son of Sir Richard Pole and Margaret Pole, 8th Countess of Salisbury, and descended through his mother from the Plantagenets — he was a great-grandson of George, Duke of Clarence, and a great-nephew of Edward IV and Richard III; he was named in honor of Saint Reginald of Orléans. This kinship with the reigning house, together with the fact that he was a distant cousin of Henry VIII, made him himself, in the eyes of many contemporaries, a latent claimant to the English throne. He studied at Oxford and then in Italy, in Padua and Venice, where he immersed himself in the humanist milieu and came into contact with the future Catholic reformers who would join him in the current of the «spirituali», which favored a spiritual renewal of the Church without rupture with Rome — among them Gasparo Contarini and Gian Pietro Carafa.

The break with Henry VIII came when the king sought the annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon and, faced with Rome's refusal, decided to assert by law the royal supremacy over the Church in England. Pole, who had already declined in 1530 the sees of York and Winchester offered by the king, withdrew to Italy in 1532 and there wrote, under pressure from Henry himself, the treatise «Pro Ecclesiasticae Unitatis Defensione» (1536), addressed to the king, in which he defended papal authority and described the break as a tyrannical and heretical act. The gesture had dramatic consequences: in reprisal, Henry had close relatives who remained in England arrested and executed — his brother, Lord Montague, in 1538, and his mother, Margaret Pole, beheaded in 1541 at an advanced age. In exile, Pole was created a cardinal on December 22, 1536, by Pope Paul III, in the order of deacons and against his own declared will, as one of the fourteen cardinals of that consistory; he would receive priestly ordination only twenty years later.

As a cardinal, he was a member of the commission chaired by Contarini that drew up the influential report «Consilium de Emendanda Ecclesia» (1537), an internal diagnosis of the abuses afflicting the Church on the eve of the Protestant Reformation. Between 1537 and 1539 he was sent on diplomatic missions to persuade the Catholic monarchies to ally against Henry VIII, attempts that failed entirely, and in 1541 he was appointed papal governor of the Patrimony of Saint Peter, taking up residence in Viterbo, where he gathered around himself a circle of spiritual reformers. From 1545, he presided as papal legate over the first sessions of the Council of Trent, withdrawing from the assembly for reasons of health before its conclusion.

After the death of Paul III on November 10, 1549, Pole was one of the leading candidates for the papacy in the following conclave, the second longest of the sixteenth century and the largest in number of electors until then (51 present at one point). The college was divided among the factions of Henry II of France, of Emperor Charles V — who supported Pole — and of the Farnese. In the vote by «accessus» of December 5, he lacked only one vote of the two thirds required; the election was not completed partly because of the intervention of Cardinal Carafa, who publicly declared that Pole was suspected of heresy and therefore ineligible, and because of the late arrival of French cardinals, which brought the deadlock back. On February 7, 1550, Cardinal Giovanni Maria Ciocchi del Monte was elected as a compromise candidate, taking the name Julius III, to whom Pole gave his vote in a decisive way.

With the accession of Mary I, the Catholic daughter of Henry VIII, in 1553, Pole returned to England as papal legate, arriving in 1554 to coordinate the formal reconciliation of the kingdom with the Church of Rome: in November of that year, in a ceremony in Parliament, he absolved the members of Parliament of the schism, repealing the laws of royal supremacy. On March 20, 1556, he was ordained a priest and, two days later, on March 22, consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury by Nicholas Heath, succeeding Thomas Cranmer — executed shortly before, on March 21, for heresy — and becoming the last Catholic archbishop to occupy that see. His last years at the head of the archdiocese were marked by growing tensions with Rome itself: the new Pope Paul IV (the same Carafa who had attacked him in the conclave), distrustful of his past among the «spirituali», revoked his papal legation in 1557 and summoned him to Rome to answer suspicions of heterodoxy — a summons that Mary I prevented from being carried out.

Historians still debate Pole's personal role in the so-called Marian persecutions, the wave of executions of Protestants for heresy that marked the reign of Mary I: some chroniclers and scholars have described him as a relatively moderate voice within the queen's ecclesiastical government, in favor of a reconciliation that privileged persuasion; other documents, however, show him urging Mary herself to use the «sword of justice» against heretics, and it falls to him, as Archbishop of Canterbury, to bear formal responsibility for the process against his predecessor Cranmer. In all, about three hundred Protestants were executed under the reign of Mary I, a number that earned the queen the historical epithet «Bloody Mary». Pole died on November 17, 1558, at Lambeth Palace, at around 7 p.m., during an influenza epidemic, about twelve hours after the queen herself — in an almost symbolic outcome. His body was taken from Lambeth to Canterbury on December 10 and buried on December 15, 1558, on the north side of the Corona (Becket's Crown) of Canterbury Cathedral, being the last prelate to be buried there; the reconciliation with Rome that he and Mary had built would be undone the very next year by the Parliament of Elizabeth I.

itens.resumo: French cardinal and chief minister of Louis XIII, architect of French royal absolutism and of the foreign policy that weakened the Habsburgs in the Thirty Years' War.
itens.corpo:
Armand Jean du Plessis was born on 9 September 1585, the fourth of five children and the last of three sons, in a family of the lesser nobility of Poitou. The exact place of his birth is a matter of debate: the baptismal certificate, drawn up in Paris on 5 May 1586, records the date and the baptism but not the place, and so historians waver between Paris and the Poitevin town now called Richelieu. His father, François du Plessis, lord of Richelieu, was a soldier and courtier, grand provost of France; his mother, Susanne de La Porte, was the daughter of a jurist. His father died of a fever during the wars of religion when Richelieu was five, leaving the family in debt. At the age of nine he was sent to the Collège de Navarre in Paris to study philosophy, and then began military training. Originally destined for arms, he found himself obliged to take the ecclesiastical path in order to keep within the family the bishopric of Luçon, a benefice the Crown had granted to his ancestors: his brother Alfred renounced the post in 1605 and withdrew to the Grande Chartreuse. In 1606, Henry IV appointed him bishop of Luçon, but since he had not yet reached the minimum canonical age (about 26), Richelieu had to travel to Rome to obtain a dispensation from Pope Paul V; he obtained it, and was consecrated bishop on 17 April 1607, a little past the age of twenty-one. In the diocese, one of the poorest in France, he became the first bishop in the country to apply the disciplinary reforms of the Council of Trent. In 1614 he was elected deputy of the clergy to the Estates General, where he stood out as a conciliating force among the three estates.

He entered the Council of State in 1616, as secretary of state for foreign and military affairs during the regency of Marie de' Medici, mother of Louis XIII, in the ministry of the favorite Concino Concini; he fell from favor the following year with the fall of the regent, being exiled first to Avignon and then sent to Rome. He managed, however, to rebuild his position as a mediator between the queen mother and the young king, which earned him the nomination to the cardinalate by Louis XIII himself — an appointment that Pope Gregory XV confirmed in 1622. In 1624 he became the king's chief minister of state, an office he would hold until his death in 1642, becoming in fact the second most powerful man in France after the monarch and earning the nickname "Red Eminence."

As a statesman, Richelieu pursued two intertwined goals: the centralization of royal power, subjecting the feudal nobility — he even banned and repressed aristocratic duels as a direct affront to the authority of the Crown — and the suppression of the political and military autonomy of the Huguenot Protestants, although he guaranteed them, by the Peace of Alès (1629), the freedom of worship already granted by the Edict of Nantes. The most dramatic episode of this policy was the siege of La Rochelle, begun on 10 September 1627 and concluded on 28 October 1628: the Huguenot fortress, center of Protestant naval power and key point of resistance to the Catholic royal government, held out for more than a year. Richelieu personally commanded the besieging troops in the king's absence and ordered the building of about twelve kilometers of trenches, eleven forts and eighteen redoubts manned by an army of thirty thousand men, as well as a dike to prevent English naval relief. The capitulation put a definitive end to Protestant political and military autonomy in France.

His position, however, was never entirely secure: on 10 November 1630, an episode known as the "Day of the Dupes" ("Journée des Dupes"), the queen mother Marie de' Medici, taking advantage of a serious illness that had nearly killed the king, demanded of Louis XIII the definitive dismissal of the cardinal, counting on the support of a devout faction of the court that saw in Richelieu an obstacle to an alliance with Catholic Spain. Against all expectations, the king chose to keep Richelieu in office — an episode that irreversibly consolidated the cardinal's predominance over any rival faction at court and sealed the political downfall of the queen mother herself.

On the international stage, he turned to weakening the Habsburg dynasty, which encircled France through Spain and the Holy Roman Empire; his central aim was to put an end to Spanish-Austrian hegemony in Europe. To this end, he did not hesitate to support, first financially and then militarily, Protestant powers — the Sweden of Gustavus Adolphus, the Protestant German principalities and the United Provinces — against the Catholic Habsburgs during the Thirty Years' War, subordinating confessional calculations to reason of state; France would enter the conflict directly in 1635. This policy earned him strong criticism within the Church itself and from the devout "party of the saints" at the French court, but it would establish France as the dominant power in Europe for the next generation.

Beyond politics, Richelieu left a lasting mark on French culture: he was provisor (rector) of the Sorbonne from 1622, promoted the reform and reconstruction of the college and its chapel — where he is buried — and founded, by royal letters patent of 29 January 1635, the Académie Française, the official literary society composed of forty members, nicknamed "the forty immortals," charged with safeguarding the purity of the French language and compiling its official dictionary, whose first edition would appear only in 1694. He died in Paris on 4 December 1642, aged 57, leaving as his political successor his protégé, Cardinal Mazarin, who would carry on a good part of his project of state.

itens.resumo: Belgian cardinal, Archbishop of Mechelen, driving force of Neo-Thomism at Leuven and a symbol of Catholic civil resistance to the German occupation of Belgium in the First World War; a pioneer of ecumenical dialogue with the Anglicans.
itens.corpo:
Désiré-Félicien-François-Joseph Mercier was born on November 21, 1851, in Braine-l'Alleud, a town near the battlefield of Waterloo, in Belgium. He studied philosophy and theology at the seminary of Mechelen and obtained the licentiate in theology from the University of Leuven in 1877, having been ordained a priest in 1874. In his first years of teaching, he taught philosophy at the Mechelen seminary itself, but it was the publication, in 1879, of Pope Leo XIII's encyclical «Aeterni Patris» — which called on the Church to retrieve the thought of Thomas Aquinas as a solid philosophical foundation in the face of modern rationalism — that defined the course of his entire intellectual career: Mercier became the most influential promoter of French-language Neo-Thomism.

In 1882 he was appointed to the first chair of Thomistic philosophy created at the University of Leuven, and from then on he worked to give this project an institutional base of its own: with the support of Leo XIII, he founded the Higher Institute of Philosophy of Leuven in 1894, of which he was the first president. The institute quickly became one of the great world centers for the renewal of scholastic thought, publishing the «Revue Néo-scolastique» (today «Revue Philosophique de Louvain») and engaging in an original way with the experimental sciences and the psychology of its time — a Thomism that did not close itself in historical repetition, but sought to answer the questions of contemporary philosophy with the conceptual tools of Saint Thomas. Consistent with this openness, he encouraged one of his disciples, Armand Thiéry, to train in experimental psychology under Wilhelm Wundt in Leipzig, and upon returning to Leuven in 1892, Thiéry founded there one of the first experimental psychology laboratories in the world — an initiative that would give rise, decades later, to the school of perception psychology associated with Albert Michotte. It was also Mercier who recognized the mathematical talent of the young Georges Lemaître, ordained him a priest on September 22, 1923, and encouraged him to study Einstein's theories of relativity, allowing him to travel to England and the United States — support without which the «primeval atom» model, which would become the first formulation of the Big Bang theory, would probably not have emerged.

Pope Saint Pius X appointed him Archbishop of Mechelen — the primatial see of Belgium — in 1906, and raised him to the cardinalate the very next year, in 1907. As archbishop, Mercier kept his intellectual activity alive, but he also took on a broader role of public leadership among Belgian Catholics, supporting Christian democracy and Catholic labor unions.

This role became central with the German invasion of Belgium in August 1914, at the beginning of the First World War. Mercier assumed a position of moral leadership in the civil resistance to the occupation: his Christmas pastoral letter of 1914, titled «Patriotisme et Endurance» («Patriotism and Endurance»), was read in all the churches of his archdiocese despite German military censorship, condemning the abuses of the occupation and reaffirming Belgium's right to independence — it resonated internationally to the point of being translated and circulated in the Allied countries as a piece of propaganda against Germany, and the cardinal himself was threatened with arrest by the occupying authorities, although he was never actually detained, probably out of fear of an international reaction. Pope Benedict XV, whose position of neutrality in the conflict was criticized by both sides, even sent him, in 1916, a letter of personal support, accompanied by his portrait, acknowledging his role in preserving the life of the Church in occupied Belgium. Mercier took part as a cardinal elector in the conclave of February 1922, which elected Pius XI.

After the war, Mercier turned to another pioneering front of work: beginning in 1921, on the initiative of the Anglican layman Lord Halifax (Charles Lindley Wood) and the French Lazarist priest Fernand Portal, and with the cautious approval of Rome, he presided over the so-called «Malines Conversations» (1921-1925), a series of informal meetings between Catholic and Anglican theologians to explore the theological conditions for a possible reunion between the two communions — the first substantial theological debates on unity between Anglicans and Catholics since the Reformation, decades before the Second Vatican Council. Mercier held that Anglicanism should be «united, not absorbed», and the conversations had the semi-tacit agreement of the Archbishop of Canterbury Randall Davidson and of Pope Pius XI. Hampered by Mercier's death and by the hostility of part of the English Catholic hierarchy, notably Cardinals Francis Bourne and Francis Aidan Gasquet, the conversations lost momentum, but they left a precedent formally resumed in 2013 by the «Malines Conversations Group» and celebrated in 2025 on the centenary of the first meeting.

Mercier died on January 23, 1926, in Brussels; some sources give the day before, January 22, for his death, owing to differing accounts of the hour of his passing. He was buried in Saint Rumbold's Cathedral in Mechelen. He had also lent decisive support to the young priest Joseph Cardijn, founder of the Young Christian Workers (YCW) — a movement which Mercier sent to study the Church's social doctrine at Leuven and which would spread, in the following decades, to dozens of countries. This combination of philosophical rigor, patriotic firmness, and social sensitivity earned Mercier, throughout his life, recognition that went beyond the boundaries of the Catholic Church itself.

itens.resumo: Hungarian cardinal, Archbishop of Esztergom and Prince Primate of Hungary, tortured and convicted in a show trial staged by the communist regime, who spent fifteen years taking refuge in the American embassy in Budapest.
itens.corpo:
József Mindszenty was born on March 29, 1892, in Csehimindszent, a small village in Vas County, then part of Austria-Hungary, the son of József Pehm and Borbála Kovács; his father was a magistrate. He studied at the Premonstratensian gymnasium in Szombathely before entering the diocesan seminary in 1911, and later adopted the name of his native village as his surname in place of the original Pehm, of Germanic origin, as a gesture of national affirmation. He was ordained a priest on June 12, 1915, the feast of the Sacred Heart, by Bishop János Mikes, and published his first book, on motherhood, in 1917. He stood out early for his opposition to authoritarian governments of every stripe: he was arrested in February 1919 under the progressive government of Mihály Károlyi and again on July 31 of that year, already under the Soviet republic of Béla Kun, for activities considered counterrevolutionary. In 1939 he urged his followers to vote against the Arrow Cross Party, and in 1940 he published the pamphlet "Green Communism," in which he described the Hungarian Nazi movement as diabolical and as evil as communism.

Consecrated Bishop of Veszprém on March 25, 1944, he was detained that same year by the pro-Nazi Arrow Cross regime, which kept him imprisoned for opposing the deportation of Hungarian Jews and for defending the autonomy of the Church. On October 2, 1945, he was appointed Archbishop of Esztergom — the primatial see of Hungary — and Prince Primate of the country, and was created a cardinal by Pope Pius XII on February 18, 1946, with the title of Cardinal Priest of Santo Stefano al Monte Celio. At the head of the Hungarian Church he became the firmest internal opponent of the Sovietization process that followed, systematically refusing to collaborate with the new communist government, unlike what would happen with part of the episcopate of other countries of the Soviet bloc.

The definitive breaking point was his refusal to accept the nationalization of Hungary's Catholic schools, imposed by the regime in 1948 as part of a broader plan of ideological control over education. On December 26, 1948, the communist political police (the ÁVH) arrested Mindszenty; shortly before, he had left in writing that he had taken part in no conspiracy and that any confession he might make would be the product of coercion. Over a period of weeks he was subjected to interrogations with sleep deprivation, beatings with rubber truncheons, and other mistreatment — methods now recognized as classic techniques for extracting forced confessions in Stalinist show trials. The trial began on February 3, 1949, and lasted three days; it was based on fabricated evidence and on a confession obtained under coercion, charging him with treason, conspiracy against the state, espionage, and illegal currency transactions, including the alleged theft of the Hungarian crown jewels and a plan to seize power after a hypothetical American invasion. On February 8, 1949, he was sentenced to life imprisonment; the six co-defendants received sentences ranging from three years to life imprisonment. The verdict drew almost unanimous international condemnation — including from governments and organizations with no particular sympathy for the Catholic Church — and prompted a United Nations resolution. Time magazine put him on its cover on February 14, 1949, under the motto "To die is to gain."

Mindszenty remained imprisoned until the Hungarian Revolution of October 1956, when he was freed on October 30 and returned to Budapest the next day, addressing the nation by radio in support of the uprising. With the return of Soviet troops and the crushing of the revolt on November 4 of that year, he followed the advice of Prime Minister Imre Nagy and took refuge in the United States embassy in Budapest, where he would remain in voluntary confinement for fifteen consecutive years — unable to leave without exposing himself to new imprisonment and, at the same time, a living symbol, for the West, of Catholic resistance to communism in Eastern Europe. The Hungarian government only allowed him to leave the country on September 28, 1971, as the result of a diplomatic agreement involving the Vatican — by then already committed, under Paul VI, to the policy of pragmatic rapprochement known as Ostpolitik —, the Hungarian government, and the American government, with the insistence of President Richard Nixon. From October 23, 1971, he lived in Vienna, as a guest of the Vatican.

Already in exile, Mindszenty refused to formally resign from the office of Archbishop of Esztergom, creating friction with Vatican diplomacy, which sought to normalize relations with the communist governments of Eastern Europe. Paul VI declared the see of Esztergom vacant in 1973, against the cardinal's will — a decision he experienced as a new wound and which would only be filled by Archbishop László Lékai in 1976. As a gesture of rapprochement, the Holy See annulled the excommunication that weighed on those involved in the trial against the cardinal and began to describe him as a "victim of history," and not of communism. Mindszenty remained firm in not recognizing the validity of the confession extorted from him, even signing it, according to accounts, while adding in Latin the expression "coactus feci" ("I did it under duress"). He published his memoirs in 1974 and died in Vienna on May 6, 1975, at the age of 83. His remains were transferred back to the Basilica of Esztergom in 1991, after the fall of communism in Hungary. The cause for beatification was opened in 1993, with the diocesan phase taking place in Esztergom between 1994 and 1996; Pope Francis declared him Venerable on February 12, 2019, recognizing his heroic virtues, and the cause now awaits the recognition of a miracle in order to advance to beatification.

itens.resumo: Croatian cardinal and Archbishop of Zagreb, convicted in a political trial by Tito's communist regime and beatified as a martyr by John Paul II in 1998.
itens.corpo:
Aloysius (Alojzije) Viktor Stepinac was born on May 8, 1898 in Brezarić, near Krašić, into a peasant family in Croatia, which was then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Drafted into the Austro-Hungarian army in 1916, he served in the First World War, was wounded, and spent five months as a prisoner of the Italians; at the end of the conflict, he returned home with the rank of lieutenant colonel and even voluntarily joined the ranks that would fight for the formation of the future Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. He decided on the priesthood only in 1924, already 26 years old, studying theology at the Gregorian University in Rome and being ordained on October 26, 1930. In the following years he founded, on his own initiative, the Caritas of the Archdiocese of Zagreb, which he came to direct.

He became coadjutor archbishop of Zagreb in 1934 and fully assumed the archdiocese in 1937, one of the most important in Croatia, becoming at age 36 the youngest bishop in Europe of his time. At its head, he lived through both the Nazi-Fascist occupation of the region during the Second World War and, at the end of the conflict, the establishment of the communist regime of Josip Broz Tito. In 1941, with the creation of the Independent State of Croatia under the Ustashe regime, an ally of the Axis, Stepinac initially welcomed the newly won Croatian autonomy and maintained formal contacts with the new government — a stance that, decades later, would fuel controversy over his role in the first months of the regime. From 1942 onward, however, he publicly denounced, in sermons and pastoral letters, the persecutions and mass killings committed by the Ustashe regime against Serbs, Jews and Roma, and his diocese came to shelter the persecuted and to carry out baptisms that, according to later testimonies, were intended to protect them — a subject on which the historical assessment and even the record of Yad Vashem have remained a matter of debate and contestation from both sides.

In February 1943 he publicly called the Jasenovac concentration camp, run by the Ustashe regime itself, a "shameful stain" and "the greatest tragedy of Croatia"; in March of the same year, after the regime ordered the imposition of the Nuremberg racial laws on the Jews of the Croatian state, he denounced the racial policies in a sermon, and in October he again declared, before thousands of the faithful, that "the Catholic Church cannot accept that races or nations, because they are great or strong, do violence to weaker races or nations" — whether they were Croats, Serbs, Jews, Roma or of any creed — having the condemnation read from the pulpits throughout Croatia. The Ustashe authorities reacted with fury: they arrested priests who had read excerpts of the sermon in their parishes, banned its publication in the press, and kept the archbishop himself under house surveillance for a few days. Historians remain divided on the real reach of these denunciations: for some, they represented the limit of what could be said publicly under a totalitarian regime allied with the Axis; for others, even taken together, they did not amount to a systematic and unequivocal condemnation of the regime while it was still in power.

With the end of the war and Tito's rise to power, Stepinac refused to accept the new regime's plan to create a national Croatian Catholic Church, subject to State control and detached from the authority of Rome — a refusal that made him a priority target of the communist persecution of the Church in Yugoslavia. Arrested on September 18, 1946, he was tried beginning on September 30 of that year in a proceeding widely regarded as political and rigged, alongside nineteen other defendants — among them former officials of the Ustashe government, such as Erih Lisak, who was sentenced to death. The charges ranged from collaboration with the occupation and dealings with the Ustashe regime to high treason against the Yugoslav State. On October 11, 1946, he was sentenced to sixteen years of forced labor; in his final defense he declared that "my conscience is clean, and the future will show that I was right." The verdict deeply divided public opinion inside and outside Yugoslavia — Winston Churchill called it an outrage against justice — and decades later, in 1985, the trial's own prosecutor, Jakov Blažević, would publicly acknowledge that the trial had been staged for a political, not a legal, purpose.

He served part of his sentence in the Lepoglava penitentiary — where, in the spring of 1953, he began to suffer from polycythemia vera, venous thrombosis and bronchial catarrh — before being transferred, on December 5, 1951, after 1,864 days in prison, to house confinement in his native village, Krašić, where he would remain under constant police surveillance for the rest of his life, forbidden to publicly exercise the episcopal ministry outside it. Pius XII named him a cardinal in January 1953, in an act of symbolic defiance toward Tito's regime, without Stepinac being able to travel to Rome to receive it, fearing he would not be allowed to return to Croatia if he left the country; in retaliation, the Yugoslav government broke off diplomatic relations with the Holy See. In 1956, Pius XII wrote to Stepinac and three other imprisoned prelates — Cardinals Stefan Wyszyński and József Mindszenty and Archbishop Josef Beran — exhorting their faithful to fidelity. Prevented by his confinement, Stepinac was unable to take part in the 1958 conclave that elected John XXIII, despite the appeals of the Episcopal Conference of Yugoslavia for his release. In a letter of June 2, 1959 to the sculptor Ivan Meštrović, he wrote: "I probably will not live to see the collapse of communism in the world, owing to my poor health. But I am absolutely certain that it will fall."

He died in Krašić on February 10, 1960, at age 61, as a result of polycythemia aggravated by the conditions of his detention, and was buried in the cathedral of Zagreb, where his tomb became a place of pilgrimage. His cause for beatification was opened on October 9, 1981; in November 1997 the Church declared him a martyr, which made it possible to waive the usual requirement of a proven miracle. On October 3, 1998, during a trip to Croatia and on the centenary of his birth, Pope John Paul II beatified him at the national shrine of Marija Bistrica, before about 500,000 faithful, presenting him as a martyr of the faith under communism. The beatification, given the persistent controversy over his conduct during the war, generated critical reactions from Serbian and Jewish sectors, remaining to this day one of the most debated causes of saints in the Church in the twentieth century.

itens.resumo: Cardinal and Vatican Secretary of State, architect of the «Ostpolitik» — the Holy See's diplomacy of pragmatic dialogue with the Communist governments of the Cold War.
itens.corpo:
Agostino Casaroli was born on November 24, 1914, in Castel San Giovanni, in the province of Piacenza, northern Italy, the son of a tailor, in a middle-class family of simple piety. He studied at the minor seminary of Bedonia, studied theology at the Alberoni College in Piacenza and canon law at the Pontifical Lateran University in Rome, between 1936 and 1940, also attending the Pontifical Ecclesiastical Academy. Ordained a priest in 1937, he entered the diplomatic service of the Holy See at a very young age, beginning as an archivist in the Secretariat of State — a career he would pursue entirely within the Roman Curia, never having governed a diocese as a residential bishop before being appointed titular archbishop of Carthage and, later, cardinal.

In February 1961, Pope John XXIII appointed him undersecretary of the Department for Extraordinary Ecclesiastical Affairs (the former office for relations with States within the Secretariat of State). From then on, and above all during the pontificate of Paul VI, he formulated and carried out the so-called Vatican «Ostpolitik»: a policy of pragmatic and discreet dialogue with the Communist governments of Eastern Europe, which placed the diplomacy of the Holy See along a line of «active neutrality» between the blocs, seeking to secure, even through tactical concessions on matters considered non-essential, some space for institutional survival for dioceses, seminaries and faithful under officially atheist regimes. His first forays behind the Iron Curtain date from 1963, when he was sent to Czechoslovakia and Hungary, ground partly prepared by Cardinal Franz König of Vienna. On September 15, 1964, he signed with the Hungarian government an agreement — whose terms were never fully published — that allowed the appointment of some bishops and the sending of seminarians to the Hungarian College in Rome, in exchange for the secularization of Catholic schools. In June 1966, in Belgrade, he signed the first of a series of agreements that gave some legality to the Catholic Church in Yugoslavia, and in 1970 he returned to the same city to sign the establishment of normal diplomatic relations with a Communist country.

The most delicate episode of this diplomacy was the case of the Hungarian Cardinal József Mindszenty, who had been living as a refugee in the American embassy in Budapest since 1956. Casaroli played a central role in his negotiated departure — the prelate left the embassy in 1971 and went into exile in Rome, which allowed the Vatican to partly normalize the situation of the Hungarian Church, but was experienced by many as the abandonment of a confessor of the faith. Then, as archbishop at the head of the Council for the Public Affairs of the Church, he led the delegation of the Holy See and presided over the opening and closing sessions of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, in Helsinki, from July 30 to August 1, 1975, at the signing of the Final Act, a document that formally committed the signatory countries — including those of the Soviet bloc — to respect human rights and fundamental freedoms, among them religious freedom, a clause that Vatican diplomacy would systematically invoke in the following years. In June 1978, already a recognized authority in international affairs, he addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

This approach already generated, even then, sharp divisions within the Church itself: cardinals and bishops who had directly suffered Communist persecution — such as Mindszenty in Hungary, or the underground bishops of Ukraine and Czechoslovakia — saw in it excessive concessions that legitimized regimes hostile to the faith and sacrificed the freedom of action of entire hierarchies in exchange for fragile guarantees; for its defenders, it was the only realistic path available to preserve the sacramental life of the Church behind the Iron Curtain, when the alternative was imposed silence or complete institutional destruction.

Created a cardinal by John Paul II on June 30, 1979, in the first consistory of that pontificate, in the same year he was appointed Vatican Secretary of State — the highest office of Vatican diplomacy after the pope —, a position he held for twelve years, until 1990, when he was succeeded by Angelo Sodano. In 1985 he became cardinal-bishop of the suburbicarian see of Porto-Santa Rufina and, from 1993 until his death, he was vice-dean of the College of Cardinals. His time in office coincided with the final phase of the Cold War and included the discreet support of the Holy See for the Polish Solidarity movement, the preparatory agreements for papal trips to countries of the Soviet bloc and, finally, the collapse of the Communist regimes of Eastern Europe between 1989 and 1991 — an outcome that, for many observers, retrospectively validated part of the diplomatic patience Casaroli had practiced for decades, even though John Paul II himself, unlike his predecessor, combined Casaroli's discreet diplomacy with a much more assertive public stance of support for Eastern Catholic dissidents.

He left office in December 1990, at almost 76 years of age, and died in Rome on June 9, 1998, of cardiorespiratory disease. Before dying, he left prepared his memoirs of the period, published posthumously in 2000 by the publisher Einaudi under the title «Il Martirio della Pazienza: la Santa Sede e i paesi comunisti (1963-1989)» («The Martyrdom of Patience: The Holy See and the Communist Countries»), with an introduction by Cardinal Achille Silvestrini, his longtime collaborator — a title that sums up, in the author's own formulation, the personal and institutional cost of that diplomacy of decades of waiting and calculated concessions. His work and method remain the subject of intense historiographical debate: for some, the architect who prepared the diplomatic ground for the democratic transitions of 1989; for others, the symbol of a diplomacy of concessions that cost too dearly the persecuted bishops and faithful whose voice was not fully defended by Rome.

itens.resumo: Nigerian cardinal, one of the highest-ranking African prelates of the contemporary Church, prefect for the universal liturgy, and named as a papabile in the 2005 conclave.
itens.corpo:
Francis Arinze was born on November 1, 1932, in Eziowelle, in the present-day state of Anambra, in southeastern Nigeria, in the Archdiocese of Onitsha, the third of seven children of Arinze Nwankwu and Bernadette Mgbafor Arinze. Born into a family of traditional Igbo religion and originally given the name Anizoba — formed from Ani, the deity of the earth and of traditions — he converted while still a boy and was baptized on his ninth birthday, November 1, 1941, by Father Cyprian Michael Iwene Tansi; this priest would be beatified by John Paul II in 1998 as the first Nigerian blessed, and in the homily of the ceremony the Pope himself mentioned, as a fruit of Tansi's ministry, that Arinze had been baptized by him. The conversion, according to biographical accounts, came from the boy's own initiative, and not from pressure by adults, the family having initially opposed it. He studied at the seminaries of Onitsha, where he had Father Tansi as his educator, and Enugu, before completing his formation in Rome. He was ordained a priest on November 23, 1958, by Archbishop Gregorio Pietro Agagianian, at the Pontifical Urban Athenaeum "De Propaganda Fide." He remained in Rome, completing his master's degree in theology in 1958 and his doctorate in sacred theology in 1960, summa cum laude: his thesis, "Igbo Sacrifice as an Introduction to the Catechesis of Holy Mass," studied sacrifice in traditional Igbo religion as a bridge to catechesis on the sacrifice of the Mass, and would be published in 1970 by Ibadan University Press under the title "Sacrifice in Ibo Religion," becoming a reference in studies on liturgical inculturation in Africa.

His ecclesiastical ascent was extraordinarily rapid: appointed on July 6, 1965, titular bishop of Fissiana and coadjutor of the Archbishop of Onitsha, he was consecrated on August 29, 1965, at the age of 32, by Archbishop Charles Heerey, thereby becoming the youngest Catholic bishop in the world. His consecration took place in time for him to take part, still as the youngest among more than 2,500 conciliar Fathers, in the final session of the Second Vatican Council in 1965 — and, according to Cardinal John Onaiyekan, he is today the only surviving Nigerian conciliar Father. He fully assumed the Archdiocese of Onitsha on June 26, 1967, right at the beginning of the Nigerian Civil War (1967-1970), a conflict that pitted the federal government against the self-proclaimed Republic of Biafra, a predominantly Igbo region to which Onitsha itself belonged — years of enormous humanitarian suffering, marked by widespread famine and mass displacement, during which Arinze had to lead his diocese under bombardment and extreme scarcity. With the war ended in 1970, he devoted himself to the material and pastoral reconstruction of the archdiocese and to a vigorous effort of evangelization that helped consolidate Onitsha as one of the regions with the highest density of Catholics in Nigeria. He was president of the Catholic Bishops' Conference of Nigeria from 1979 to 1984.

Called to Rome by Pope John Paul II, he was appointed on April 8, 1984, pro-prefect of the then Secretariat for Non-Christians, renamed the Pontifical Council for Interreligious Dialogue, which he would lead until 2002. He was created a cardinal in the consistory of May 25, 1985, as Cardinal-Deacon of San Giovanni della Pigna — an order that, in 1996, became Cardinal-Priest, and which since 2005 he has held as Cardinal-Bishop of Velletri-Segni, one of the suburbicarian sees reserved for cardinal-bishops. He left the Archdiocese of Onitsha on March 9, 1985. In Rome, he also served as prefect of the Congregation for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments from 2002 to 2008, the dicastery responsible for overseeing the liturgy throughout the Latin Church, a position in which he became known for defending a liturgical celebration marked by reverence and fidelity to the rubrics, including expressed reservations about certain post-conciliar liturgical innovations that he considered to depart from the spirit of the reform intended by the Second Vatican Council. It was under his signature, as prefect, that the Congregation published the instruction "Redemptionis Sacramentum," a normative document on the correct celebration of the Mass and the worship of the Eucharist in view of the liturgical abuses then reported in different parts of the world: approved by John Paul II on March 19, 2004, the Solemnity of Saint Joseph, and signed on March 25, the Solemnity of the Annunciation, it was presented by Arinze himself at a press conference at the Vatican on April 22, 2004, as a disciplinary development of the encyclical "Ecclesia de Eucharistia," which had diagnosed, after the conciliar liturgical reform, "abuses stemming from a misguided sense of creativity and adaptation." He is the author of numerous books on spirituality and pastoral theology — among them "Sacrifice in Ibo Religion," "The Church in Dialogue: Walking with Other Believers," "Religions for Peace," "Meeting Other Believers," and "The Evangelizing Parish" — and has received several honorary doctorates, including from the Catholic University of America (1998) and the University of Nigeria (1986), as well as the Grand Cross of the Order of the Niger, one of Nigeria's highest civil honors.

As one of the most visible faces of the African episcopate in the Roman Curia, his name circulated insistently among the papabili in the 2005 conclave, which would elect Benedict XVI — speculation that the international press amplified as a concrete possibility of the election of a non-European pope in the modern era, a hypothesis that would only come true eight years later, in 2013, with the election of the Argentine Jorge Mario Bergoglio. Arinze took part as an elector in the 2005 conclave and remained a cardinal elector until he turned 80 on November 1, 2012, ceasing to be a voter in 2013. Already in his nineties, he continued to speak out publicly in defense of the faith and to travel for conferences — in November 2024, at the age of 92, he traveled alone to Nigeria to speak at Bigard Memorial Seminary in Enugu — and he remains to this day one of the most respected and sought-after figures of the African Catholic hierarchy.

itens.resumo: Cuban cardinal, Archbishop of Havana for nearly 35 years, a protagonist of the dialogue between the Catholic Church and the Cuban State and mediator of the secret negotiations that restored ties between Cuba and the United States in 2014.
itens.corpo:
Jaime Lucas Ortega y Alamino was born on October 18, 1936, in Jagüey Grande, in the Cuban province of Matanzas, the son of a sugar mill worker who later became a merchant. He completed his primary education at the Arturo Echemendía school and his secondary education at the Instituto Superior de Estudios Secundarios de Matanzas, obtaining in 1955 a diploma in arts and sciences. In 1956 he entered the Seminary of San Alberto Magno in Matanzas, run by the Priests of the Quebec Foreign Missions Society, still under the government of Fulgencio Batista; after four years of humanities and philosophy, he was sent by the diocese to study theology at the Foreign Missions Seminary in Laval, Quebec, Canada. He returned to Cuba, by then under the revolutionary regime of Fidel Castro, established in 1959, and was ordained a priest on August 2, 1964, in the Cathedral of Matanzas, by Bishop José Maximino Eusebio Domínguez y Rodríguez.

His early ministry, as parochial vicar in Cárdenas, was interrupted as early as 1966: Ortega was detained and sent for about eight months to one of the forced labor camps known by the acronym UMAP (Unidades Militares de Ayuda a la Producción, Military Units to Aid Production), which the Cuban government then imposed on priests, seminarians, homosexuals, Jehovah's Witnesses and other groups considered socially undesirable or politically suspect by the regime. He spoke publicly about this episode almost fifty years later, in a 2014 interview, in which he said it was "a unique experience in the life of a priest" that placed him "in the midst of the people." At the end of his internment, in 1967, he was appointed pastor of his hometown, Jagüey Grande, where, like almost all Cuban priests of the time, few in number and overburdened, he was responsible for the care of several parishes at once. In 1969 he became pastor of the Cathedral of Matanzas, while also serving the parish of Pueblo Nuevo and two rural churches, in addition to presiding over the Diocesan Catechesis Commission and founding a youth movement with summer camps and evangelization through theater. He also taught moral theology at the Interdiocesan Seminary of San Carlos and San Ambrosio in Havana for several years.

Appointed Bishop of Pinar del Río by Pope John Paul II on December 4, 1978, and consecrated on January 14, 1979, by Archbishop Mario Tagliaferri, he was promoted on November 21, 1981, to the metropolitan see of San Cristóbal de Havana, the most important in the country. He presided over the Conference of Catholic Bishops of Cuba in 1988-1998 and again in 2001-2007, was second vice-president of the Latin American Episcopal Council (CELAM) between 1995 and 1999, and was a consultor of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America. He was created a cardinal by John Paul II in the consistory of November 26, 1994, receiving the title of Cardinal-Priest of Santi Aquila e Priscilla, and thus became the second Cuban in history to receive the cardinal's biretta; the first had been Archbishop Manuel Arteaga y Betancourt, created by Pius XII in 1946. He took part as an elector in the conclaves of 2005, which elected Benedict XVI, and of 2013, which elected Francis.

As Archbishop of Havana, he handled the relationship between the Church and an officially atheist State with notable caution, maintaining a direct and discreet dialogue with the authorities that, over the decades, gradually opened small spaces of religious freedom. Concrete measures date from this effort, such as the reinstatement of the Christmas holiday, suspended in Cuba since 1968 so as not to interrupt the sugarcane harvest: at the request of John Paul II himself, made to Fidel Castro at the Vatican in the autumn of 1996, Castro announced on December 13, 1997, the restoration of the holiday that very year, a gesture that preceded the papal visit. That historic visit of John Paul II to Cuba, in January 1998, the first by a pope to the country, from the 21st to the 26th of that month, relied on Ortega's personal coordination with the government, paving the way for the next two papal visits, also arranged by him: that of Benedict XVI, in March 2012, and that of Francis, in September 2015.

In his last years at the head of the archdiocese, he played a role now widely recognized as a behind-the-scenes interlocutor in the secret negotiations that led to the surprise announcement of the restoration of diplomatic relations between Cuba and the United States on December 17, 2014, after more than five decades of rupture. Ortega himself narrated the process in detail in the book "Encuentro, diálogo y acuerdo. El papa Francisco, Cuba y Estados Unidos" (2017): Francis entrusted him with two letters, one for Raúl Castro and another for Barack Obama, which were in his hands from June 25, 2014, and whose delivery by hand to Obama took place in absolute secrecy; when the magazine "Espacio Laical" asked him to publish the texts, he replied: "Yo era la carta" ("I was the letter"). The talks, begun in 2013, continued in Canada, with Colonel Alejandro Castro Espín, son of Raúl, leading the Cuban delegation and Ricardo Zúñiga leading the American one, until the agreement was signed at the Vatican; the date of the announcement was chosen as a tribute to Pope Francis's birthday. Ortega publicly advocated greater religious and civil freedom for Cubans and at the same time criticized the American economic embargo against the island, a position that exposed him to criticism both from the more conservative sectors of the Cuban exile community, who accused him of excessive accommodation to the regime, and, occasionally, from internal dissidents who wanted more confrontational positions from him. Still under his leadership, the Father Félix Varela Cultural Center was inaugurated in 2011 in the former building of the San Carlos and San Ambrosio seminary where he had taught decades earlier; from 2012 it would also house the magazine "Espacio Laical." He submitted his resignation as Archbishop of Havana on October 18, 2011, due to age limit; the resignation was accepted by Francis on April 26, 2016, and he was succeeded by Juan de la Caridad García Rodríguez, a native of Camagüey. Ortega died in Havana on July 26, 2019, at the age of 82, remembered as the most influential ecclesiastical figure of the Cuban Church in several generations.

itens.resumo: The secluded gathering of the cardinal electors charged with electing the new Bishop of Rome, now governed by the apostolic constitution «Universi Dominici Gregis».
itens.corpo:
The word «conclave» — from the Latin «cum clave», «with a key» — goes back to the episode that gave rise to the current form of papal election: the succession of Pope Clement IV, who died in November 1268, dragged on for nearly three years amid disputes between rival political factions within the College of Cardinals, gathered in the episcopal palace of Viterbo. Faced with the paralysis, the citizens of Viterbo — exasperated by the cost of supporting the delegation and pressed by the captain of the people, Raniero Gatti — took drastic measures: they locked the cardinal electors in under key and finally removed the roof of the hall where they were gathered, exposing them to the elements in order to force a decision. The election, the longest in history, lasted about thirty-three months and ended on September 1, 1271, with the choice of Teobaldo Visconti — then archdeacon of Liège, who was neither a cardinal nor even a priest — who took the name Gregory X.

Marked by his own experience, Gregory X formally established on July 7, 1274, in the bull «Ubi Periculum», promulgated during the Second Council of Lyons, the basic rules of the conclave that would shape all subsequent papal elections: complete isolation of the cardinal electors, literally locked in «with a key» both from inside and outside, without communication with the outside world, and progressive restriction of food if the election dragged on beyond a few days. The adoption was supported by the hundreds of bishops gathered at the council, against the objection of the cardinals themselves. The first conclave held under these rules was that of January 1276, which elected Innocent V in only one day. Its application, however, was soon suspended by Adrian V and formally revoked by John XXI on September 20, 1276; the following elections, held without a conclave, were long and drawn out — that of Celestine V, in 1292-1294, took more than two years. It was necessary for Boniface VIII, in 1298, to incorporate the «Ubi Periculum» into canon law for the format to be definitively consolidated.

One of the best-known signs of the process, the smoke that announces the result of each vote, has a relatively recent origin: white smoke as a clear and unmistakable indication of a completed election was only consolidated from 1914 onward, after Pope Pius X determined, in 1904, that the notes and other papers used in the voting — and not only the ballots — should also be burned along with them at the end of each scrutiny, producing white smoke in sufficient quantity to be seen clearly by the faithful in Saint Peter's Square; before that, the distinction between smoke of a positive and negative result was often ambiguous. Other formalities accumulated over time: in 1621, Gregory XV introduced the requirement of a secret, written vote; in 1904, Pius X abolished any alleged right of exclusion claimed by monarchs and imposed secrecy on everything that occurs in the conclave, even after its end.

Today's discipline is set out in the apostolic constitution «Universi Dominici Gregis», promulgated by John Paul II on February 22, 1996 and later adjusted by Benedict XVI, in 2007 and 2013, and by Francis. Only the cardinal electors who have not reached their eightieth birthday on the day the See becomes vacant may vote — an age limit set by Paul VI in the motu proprio «Ingravescentem Aetatem», of 1970, which removed from octogenarian cardinals the right to enter a conclave — in an electoral college limited to a maximum of 120 cardinals. The voting takes place in the Sistine Chapel, under an oath of absolute secrecy reinforced by severe canonical penalties, with the count verified by three cardinal scrutineers chosen by lot for each vote; up to four scrutinies are held per day — two in the morning and two in the afternoon — and a valid election always requires a two-thirds majority of the votes, a principle taken up again from the Third Lateran Council (1179). Benedict XVI, in 2007, reestablished that even after thirty-three scrutinies the election continues to require two thirds, eliminating the loophole introduced by John Paul II that allowed, after that number, election by absolute majority. Francis, for his part, in creating more than 120 cardinal electors, waived the clause on the numerical limit on the basis of «Universi Dominici Gregis» itself, so that all cardinals under eighty years of age retained the right to vote. The black smoke, produced by burning the ballots without a conclusive result, or white, when a name finally gathers the required majority — now reinforced by the ringing of the bells of Saint Peter's, a measure adopted precisely to eliminate any residual ambiguity — remains the most awaited public sign of the process for the faithful gathered in the square.

The isolation still begins today with the ritual cry «extra omnes» («everybody out»), which expels from the Sistine Chapel all who are not cardinal electors, and ends with the solemn announcement «Habemus Papam!», made from the central loggia of Saint Peter's Basilica by the cardinal protodeacon — as happened on March 13, 2013, when Cardinal Jean-Louis Tauran announced to the world, at the end of the fifth scrutiny, the election of the Argentine archbishop Jorge Mario Bergoglio, who would take the name Francis. John Paul II's constitution also clarified, in an unprecedented way, which matters may be dealt with by the College of Cardinals during the vacancy of the See and which remain reserved exclusively to the future pope — reinforcing that the administration of this interregnum is strictly ordinary, without power to innovate in the government of the Church, and formally transferring to the College of Cardinals, and not only to the cardinal camerlengo alone, the administrative authority of the Holy See while the chair of Peter is vacant.
